newsitem.title: USA: Digital to return secret chip papers to Intel.
newsitem.headline: Digital to return secret chip papers to Intel.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp., capitulating to part of a lawsuit by Intel Corp., has agreed to return secret documents to Intel about a powerful chip that company has in the works, a Digital spokesman said.

The secret documents outline Intel's technical and marketing plan for Merced, a next-generation microprocessor that Intel is expected to unveil in a few years. Computer makers, including Digital, rely on information in such confidential Intel documents to plan new lines of personal computers.
A spokesman for Digital, which is based in Maynard, Mass., said the company had not yet returned the Merced documents, but has decided it will return them.

"We intend to return the documents," the spokesman, Dan Kaferle, told Reuters. He said Digital had no plans to work with Intel on developing the Merced when Digital's own Alpha processor has been on the market for years.
"They are more than a year old and were provided so Digital could provide critical feedback to Intel on their Merced design process," he said of the documents.

"We have no need for this information and are not participating in developing Intel's much delayed 64-bit processor," he said. "Our 64-bit processor has been on the market for five years and we're not interested in helping them design the chip, so the information is irrelevant to us."

Despite its lengthy lead in marketing processors based on an architecture faster than existing 32-bit processors, Digital still ships far more computers that contain Intel chips than are outfitted with its own Alphas.
The fight over the documents arose after Digital sued Intel in May, alleging the chip maker stole key semiconductor secrets from it and had infringed on a handful of Digital semiconductor patents.
Intel retaliated by suing to force Digital to give back all sensitive documents Intel had shared with Digital.
People close to the litigation between the companies said Digital was keeping confidential documents about upcoming Intel Pentium II chips.
Digital said it would keep materials that were part of Intel's normal communications with computer makers.
"It is not our intention to return other materials which Intel routinely supplies to other computer manufacturers," Kaferle said of the other documents.

Analysts have said Digital could be at a huge disadvantage to competitors such as International Business Machines Corp., Compaq Computer Corp. and Hewlett-Packard Co., Intel's initial Merced partner, if it were denied access to Intel's plans. Intel, based in Santa Clara, Calif., is still pursuing its lawsuit to get back the remaining documents, a spokesman said.
"We asked that the date of the hearing be moved out to September," said Intel spokesman Chuck Malloy. "This changes nothing about the lawsuit."
